market_context: United States/general English; refrigeration of raw egg contents outside the shell
title: How long does an opened raw egg last in the fridge?

seo.title: How long does an opened raw egg last in the fridge?
seo.meta_description: Raw egg whites and yolks keep 2–4 days refrigerated at 40 °F or below. A prepared raw-egg mixture should generally be cooked within 24 hours.
seo.search_intent: Learn how long a cracked raw egg, white, yolk or raw egg mixture can be refrigerated.

excerpt: Once an egg is cracked, the shell no longer protects it. USDA lists 2–4 refrigerated days for raw whites and yolks at 40 °F or below. If the egg is already mixed into a raw dish, USDA recommends cooking immediately or refrigerating and cooking within 24 hours.
content_html:
An intact refrigerated shell egg can last for weeks, but an opened egg has a much shorter window. USDA lists 2–4 days for raw whites and yolks held at 40 °F or below.

What counts as an opened egg?

Once the shell is cracked and the contents are transferred to a clean container, treat them as raw egg outside its protective shell. Cover and refrigerate promptly.

Whites and yolks: 2–4 days

USDA's storage chart gives 2–4 days for both raw egg whites and raw yolks. That is far shorter than the 3–5 weeks listed for intact refrigerated shell eggs.

Raw egg mixtures should be used sooner

If the egg has already been mixed into a batter, coating, omelet mixture or another dish that will be cooked later, USDA recommends cooking immediately or refrigerating and cooking within 24 hours.

Use a clean covered container

Do not try to return the egg to a broken shell. The shell no longer provides a useful barrier and can introduce contamination.

Can opened egg be frozen?

Raw whites freeze well; USDA lists up to a year. Yolks become thick and gel-like if frozen plain. FDA recommends beating yolks and whites together before freezing whole raw egg.

Why breaking the shell changes the storage window so much

While intact, the shell and its membranes form a physical barrier and the egg remains a closed unit. Once cracked, that protection is gone and the contents are exposed to utensils, hands, air and the storage container. The jump from weeks to only a few days is therefore not contradictory.

If you use only part of an egg, do not leave the remainder in an open bowl. Transfer it promptly to a clean covered container, mark the date and keep it in a consistently cold part of the refrigerator rather than the door.

Once an egg has been cracked, the practical question is no longer how long shell eggs keep but how the exposed white or yolk has been handled. Refrigeration slows bacterial growth, yet it does not restore the protection provided by the shell and its membranes. A clean container with a tight lid matters because it limits contact with hands, utensils, drips and odors from other foods. Dating the container is also useful: raw whites and yolks are easy to forget because they may look unchanged for several days even when the recommended storage window is already ending.

The 2–4 day refrigerator window is best treated as a planning limit rather than a promise that every cracked egg will remain suitable until the last hour of day four. If the egg sat on the counter during cooking, was transferred with a dirty utensil or came from a shell that was already damaged, its real margin may be shorter. Keep the refrigerator at 40 °F or below and store the container on an interior shelf instead of the door, where temperatures fluctuate more. If you cannot remember when the egg was cracked, discarding it is safer than trying to reconstruct the timeline from appearance alone.

Separated yolks and whites also behave differently in the kitchen even though their refrigerated storage guidance is similar. Whites generally remain pourable and can later be cooked or frozen. Yolks tend to thicken as they stand and are more troublesome to freeze plain because their texture can become gel-like. That is a quality issue rather than a reason to leave them unrefrigerated. If the goal is to save unused egg for baking, freezing the whites or freezing beaten whole egg can be more practical than stretching refrigerator storage to its limit.

Smell and appearance can identify obvious spoilage, but they cannot prove that a raw egg is microbiologically safe. A normal-looking egg may still contain pathogens, which is why time, temperature and cooking matter more than a sniff test. For dishes that will be eaten raw or lightly cooked, pasteurized eggs or pasteurized egg products offer an additional safety margin. For ordinary cooking, keep the leftover raw egg cold, use it promptly and cook it thoroughly. The simplest routine is to crack only what you need; when that is not possible, cover, date and refrigerate the remainder immediately.

Bottom line

Use 2–4 days for a cracked raw egg or separated white/yolk, and aim for 24 hours when it is already part of a prepared raw mixture.

faq.question: Can I use a cracked egg after 3 days?
faq.answer: Three days is within USDA's 2–4 day refrigerator guidance if it stayed at 40 °F or below in a clean covered container.

faq.question: How long does raw egg white last in the fridge?
How long can an uncooked omelet mixture be refrigerated?
faq.answer: USDA advises cooking raw egg dishes immediately or refrigerating and cooking within 24 hours.
